appraisal.identified_item: Mixed lot: four Chinese export 'rose medallion'/famille rose porcelain plates (unmarked), a bronze charcoal-heated 'silk iron' (smoothing iron), and a cloisonné-decorated bronze/metal candlestick or stand
appraisal.reasoning: This is an unmarked mixed lot with no identifiable maker, workshop, or reign mark on any piece — the plate backs (photo 2) are plain white porcelain, which rules out attribution to a specific kiln or period and undercuts the 'Qing Dynasty' claim in the title (auction house titles routinely overstate age on unmarked Chinese export ware). Rose medallion/famille rose plates in this decorative, mismatched-pattern style are extremely common at auction — genuine 19th c. examples exist, but the vivid, slightly heavy enamel and uniform gilt scalloped borders seen here are typical of the abundant 20th c. decorator-market production, which is what I'm valuing this as absent contrary evidence. The bronze 'silk iron' and cloisonné-enameled candlestick/stand are minor curios with modest individual value ($30–80 typical range for such small bronze/cloisonné curios at general estate auctions). As a bundled lot of unmarked decorative pieces, this realistically lands in the $150–250 range at a mixed-lot estate auction like EBTH; the $111 current bid across 13 bidders with 43 hours left suggests it will likely finish within or slightly above that band. I have no specific realized comps for this maker/lot since no maker is identifiable — reporting an empty comps list rather than inventing sales, per the 'name the market, not the calibre' principle. Confidence is capped low (0.3) because age/authenticity of the porcelain cannot be confirmed from photos and no comparable named-maker sales exist to anchor the estimate.
appraisal.style_era: Chinese export decorative ware, style associated with late Qing (19th c.) but more likely Republic-period or 20th c. decorator reproductions given lack of reign marks and mass-market decoration

Other pieces (clock, jasperware box, onyx dish, cut-glass tray) appear intact and undamaged from the images provided.
appraisal.identified_item: Mixed decor lot: crystal vase attributed to George Thompson for Steuben, Hoya crystal desk clock, Wedgwood-style blue jasperware lidded box, cut-crystal coaster/tray with engraved cherub scene, onyx triangular dish, footed glass tumbler, and a crimped-rim glass bowl
appraisal.maker_guess: Steuben (vase, attributed to designer George Thompson); Hoya (clock); Wedgwood-style jasperware maker unconfirmed
appraisal.reasoning: This is a multi-item lot, and value is driven almost entirely by the Steuben attribution on the vase. Steuben produced huge volumes of unadorned, acid-etch-signed crystal vases from the 1930s-1980s; at auction these commonly realize modest sums ($40-150) unless tied to a documented, named Thompson pattern (e.g., 'Flame,' 'Gazelle' forms), which usually needs paperwork or a distinctive silhouette to command more. I cannot recall specific realised comps for 'George Thompson for Steuben' vases in this exact form, so I'm treating it as a generic Steuben vase rather than a documented Thompson design, and confidence is capped accordingly. The Hoya desk clock is a decent but not collectible brand (typically $15-40 at auction). The jasperware box, onyx dish, cut-glass cherub coaster, tumbler, and bowl are all ordinary decorative smalls that individually bring $10-30 each at estate auction. Summed and discounted for a mixed lot (buyers pay less per-item for grab-bag lots than for single pieces), I land near $90 total hammer. Given the $1 opening bid and 44 hours remaining, there's room for this to move up as bidders recognize the Steuben name, but I'd be cautious overpaying since 'Steuben' alone doesn't guarantee a premium without a notable form or paperwork — I'm deliberately returning the lower end of plausible outcomes.
appraisal.style_era: Mid-20th-century American modern (Steuben) mixed with later 20th-century Japanese crystal (Hoya) and assorted tabletop glass/decor

appraisal.identified_item: Mixed lot of weighted sterling silver table accessories: pair of weighted-sterling compotes/candy dishes with scalloped pressed-glass liners, one small weighted-sterling pincushion (shell-form, pierced rim, velvet insert) attributed to Gorham, one small weighted-sterling pepper caster, and a pair of weighted-sterling gadroon-base candlesticks
appraisal.maker_guess: Gorham (per title, for at least the pincushion; other pieces likely unmarked or by other American weighted-sterling makers such as Duchin, Frank Whiting, or Empire — not independently confirmed from photos)
appraisal.reasoning: All of these are WEIGHTED sterling — a thin sterling shell over a cement/plaster core for stability — which is standard for mid-century candlesticks, compotes and small novelty pieces like pincushions and casters. That construction caps scrap value (only a fraction of the piece is actual silver) and caps collector value too, since weighted sterling of this common Colonial-Revival gadroon/shell styling is mass-produced and unremarkable compared to Gorham's flatware or hollowware patterns that command real premiums. I cannot recall specific realized auction prices for this exact Gorham pincushion or for these specific compote/candlestick forms, so I'm not fabricating comps — genuinely unlisted at the individual-model level in what I can verify. Based on the general pattern for weighted-sterling lots of this type at estate auction houses (small pincushions and casters typically realize $15-40 each, weighted candlestick pairs $25-50, glass-insert weighted compote pairs $30-70), a bundled lot like this plausibly lands in the $60-120 range at hammer. Current bid of $6 across 4 bids with 48 hours left is consistent with early-stage bidding on this class of lot, not a signal of low ultimate value. As-is value reflects sale in current tarnished state with no polishing; restoration here is just a light hand-polish, not a real value driver, so I kept the restored uplift modest and did not let it leak into the as-is figure. Confidence is capped at 0.3 given the lack of maker-specific realized comps.
appraisal.style_era: American mid-20th century (c. 1930s-1950s), traditional/Colonial Revival weighted sterling tableware

appraisal.condition_assessment: No visible chips, cracks, or hairlines in the photos; stopper appears to fit the neck properly; polish and clarity look good with no cloudiness. Base mark not visible/confirmable in photos, but form and cut pattern are consistent with genuine Waterford Lismore.
appraisal.identified_item: Waterford "Lismore" pattern cut crystal ship's decanter with wedge/diamond cut wide base and faceted ball stopper
appraisal.reasoning: Pattern and form (diamond/wedge cut, flat wide 'ship's' base for stability, faceted ball stopper) are textbook Waterford Lismore, a well-documented and sought-after pattern, so I'm confident in the maker/pattern ID even without a clearly visible base mark. This house's own recent Lismore results are the primary comp: goblets realized $110 (16 bids), old fashioneds $120 (10 bids), bowls $52 (8 bids), and double-old-fashioned/shot glasses only $13 (4 bids) — showing Lismore barware at this venue clears in the $50-$120 range depending on piece desirability, with sets of glasses doing better than single mixed lots. A ship's decanter is a larger, more substantial single-item form than stemware but is still a common Waterford piece (not rare), so I'd expect it to land near the middle-to-upper end of that range rather than dramatically above it. Current bidding of $31 across 9 bids with 43 hours left is consistent with this trajectory — EBTH lots often see most bid activity in the final hours, and the goblet/old-fashioned comps show meaningful late movement. I'm estimating a realised hammer of roughly $100-120, in line with the goblet and old-fashioned comps rather than assuming a decanter premium I can't support with a specific realised comp. No restoration is applicable to crystal in sound condition, so as-is and restored values are the same. Deal score is middling: not undervalued given current bid trajectory look reasonable relative to comps, but not overpriced either.
appraisal.style_era: Modern Waterford Lismore line, mid-late 20th century production (pattern introduced 1952, still in production)
